 Early voting sustained high voter turnout during the midterms 
 By Taylor Sansom, The Shorthorn editor-in-chief 
 Taylor Sansom 
 Editor-in-chief
 Author email

 2 hrs ago

 People walk outside during early voting Oct. 21 at the Tarrant County Sub-Courthouse in Arlington. 
 Photo by Emmanuel Pizano 
 Early voting for the midterm election at UTA brought vans, bicycles and student-led marches.
 The loss of the Maverick Activities Center as a voting site prompted campus organizations and nonprofits to assist students and community members in casting their ballots at the Tarrant County Sub-Courthouse in Arlington on Abram Street. For many, the efforts provided a push to get them to the polls.
 Industrial engineering sophomore Hans Nguyen said in previous Shorthorn reporting that the vans provided by Student Government, Delta Sigma Theta, Omega Psi Phi and Mount Olive Baptist Church lowered the barriers of resistance for voting.
 Across various Texas counties, the early voting period — from Oct. 19 to Oct. 30 — had a high turnout.
 This article was featured in the Nov. 4 print 
 More than 7.7 million of the 19 million registered Texan voters participated in early voting for the 2026 midterm election, according to preliminary data from the secretary of state’s office.
 Over 1.8 million people across North Texas voted: Dallas County saw 607,886 voters, Collin County had 374,250 and Denton County had 319,081, according to each county’s website.
 Tarrant County saw 571,950 ballots out of its 1.2 million registered voters, according to the county website.
 Janet Mattern, president of the League of Women Voters of Tarrant County, said the high turnout was encouraging.
 “This is Texas. I’m always impressed when voters turn out,” Mattern said.
 High voter turnout tends to indicate that people are paying attention to the issues that are impacting their lives and communities, she said. For Tarrant County, Mattern said, the high turnout might be sending a message to elected county leaders that the people have the power.
 “Voters know that it’s their civic duty to make their voices heard through voting,” she said.
 A midterm election happens two years into a president’s four-year term. For Texans, this year’s ballot was composed of federal, state and local roles such as governor, U.S. Senate seats, state judges and county commissioners.
 During this year’s midterm, there were fewer polling locations for voters.
 The decision to remove the MAC as a polling location came from a Sept. 1 Tarrant County Commissioners Court meeting. The proximity of the center to the sub-courthouse was cited as the reason for the site’s removal, according to previous Shorthorn reporting.
 Republican leaders have called the move to reduce sites a cost-saving measure. During the Sept. 1 meeting, Tarrant County Judge Tim O’Hare said that during the most recent general election, multiple polling locations were empty, according to previous Shorthorn reporting.
 The sites’ removal sparked many students into action.
 “Even though Tarrant County took away our voting location, they didn’t take away our voice,” Student Body President Andres Morales said. “This created a fuel for students and for citizens.”
 Three vans transported students between the Tarrant County Sub-Courthouse in Arlington and the University Center for the second day of early voting, according to previous Shorthorn reporting.
 The service’s success led to its extension.
 By the end of the early voting period, the vans had assisted around 250 students to the courthouse, Morales said.
 He said the university has around 10,000 students living on campus, many of them relying on MavMover shuttle buses to get around.
 “If students who lived on campus two years ago who still live on campus now didn’t have a means of transportation, meaning they can’t go to the MAC anymore to vote, how were they going to get to the Tarrant County courthouse to go vote?” Morales said.
 Jaysen Johnson, chair for community affairs and senator for the College of Liberal Arts, said he hopes this election continues the argument of bringing the MAC back as a voting location for later elections.
 “It’s not just students using that location,” Johnson said. “When I went myself the last two times, I saw people in all different demographics.”
 Despite the site’s removal — along with three others during the early voting period — Tarrant County saw the highest early voting turnout during a midterm election in its history.
 Across the 12 days of early voting, Oct. 30 saw the highest turnout, with over 60,000 people participating across Tarrant County. The lowest voter turnout day was Oct. 25, when around 24,500 voters participated.
 Johnson said the current political landscape, gas prices and the cost of living could have contributed to the high turnout across the county. He said there’s a consensus on the policies and positions the younger generation cares about, which could be reflected in the results of future elections, he said.
 Mattern said the more people that show up to the polls, the better.
 “Voting should be for hoping for something better, hoping for making a change,” she said.
